name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,158

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing; the grid proves the blog's enumeration wrong at 11 across, recounted from the answer here

clue.text: One time writer’s countryman

indicators.note: asking for just one of a doubled letter means the second copy has to go

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
Sir Walter Scott, the Waverley novelist, whose surname ends in a double letter

explanation.surface: A literary note about a former author and the man from his homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One time' reads like 'former', but it means one T: SCOTT keeps only one of its two Ts, leaving SCOT. The writer's countryman is a fellow Scotsman, so the surface is nearly an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: Countryman here means a compatriot, someone born in the same nation, and Walter Scott's nation was Scotland.

clue.text: He re-imagined Notting Hill converted to trenches

indicators.note: converting something turns it into a different form, so the letters take a new order

blocks.note: the ten letters of these two words are the raw material

explanation.surface: Someone imagines a London district turned into a battlefield of dug-in trenches.
explanation.walkthrough: G. K. Chesterton wrote The Napoleon of Notting Hill, a fantasy of a future London where the borough goes to war; Notting Hill is a district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: His 1904 novel reinvents a real London neighbourhood as an independent city-state fighting its neighbours, so describing the author by that book identifies him.

clue.text: Giant caught out by a fairy

indicators.note: a player who is out leaves the field, so that letter departs from the word

blocks.note: titanic is an adjective meaning enormous
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
taken as written

explanation.surface: A huge creature is defeated, taken by surprise by a fairy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giant' looks like a noun (TITAN), but it is the adjective TITANIC; losing its C and adding A gives TITANIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Titania is queen of the fairies in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, so she is a named example of a fairy.

clue.text: “Offshore author” sounds apt for Durrell

indicators.note: this verb tells us to listen to the phrase rather than read its spelling

blocks.note: something apt for a person fits them, and Durrell the naturalist was called Gerald

explanation.surface: A wry suggestion that the phrase 'offshore author' suits Gerald Durrell, who wrote about island life on Corfu.
explanation.walkthrough: Penelope Fitzgerald won the Booker Prize with Offshore, set on Thames houseboats. Durrell fits the surface because he wrote of Corfu, but it is his first name that matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Offshore is the title of Penelope Fitzgerald's 1979 Booker-winning novel, so its writer is the person meant.

clue.text: Backtracking of an island assembly

indicators.note: going back over one's tracks means travelling the other way, so the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: taken as written
Rùm is a small island of the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland

explanation.surface: A political gathering on an island retreats from its earlier position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backtracking' sounds like a politician's U-turn, but it only reverses the little word next to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A forum is a meeting or gathering for public discussion, named after the Roman marketplace where citizens debated.

clue.text: Knights may appear in these, thanks to poets

blocks.note: ta is informal British for thank you
bard is a traditional word for a poet

explanation.surface: Thanks to poets, chivalrous heroes turn up in verse romances.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests knights appearing in poems thanks to poets; in fact 'appear in' means to be seen wearing. Ta is everyday British slang for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabard is the sleeveless tunic worn over armour and bearing a coat of arms, so knights were dressed in them.

clue.text: Revered or famous poem, Gray initially fibbed about

indicators.note: something done initially happens at the start, so only the opening letter is wanted
to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: the poet Thomas Gray's name begins with this letter
to fib is to tell a small lie
taken as written
Kipling's If— is one of the best-known poems in English

explanation.surface: A celebrated poem by Thomas Gray turns out to have stretched the truth.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray makes one think of his Elegy, but the famous poem meant is Kipling's two-letter If—, among the best-loved poems in English.
explanation.definitionFit: Glorified and revered are both past participles meaning held in very high honour or praised as worthy of worship.

clue.text: Attar came up with work that’s timeless

indicators.note: being without time means the abbreviation for time is taken away

blocks.note: past tense of rise, to come up
toil is hard work

explanation.surface: Attar, the Persian poet of The Conference of the Birds, produced a work that has never dated.
explanation.walkthrough: In a literary puzzle Attar looks like the Sufi poet Farid ud-Din Attar; here it is the perfume. Losing T, the time abbreviation, from TOIL leaves OIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Attar is an essential oil distilled from flower petals, most famously from damask roses, so attar of roses is this fragrant oil.

clue.text: One responsible for Brunetti’s Christmas being over

indicators.note: something turned over is flipped, so the letters are flipped end to end

blocks.note: Noel is another word for Christmas

explanation.surface: The Venetian detective Brunetti's Christmas has come to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christmas being over' looks like the season ending; it is NOEL turned over. The 's is 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Donna Leon is the American novelist who created Commissario Guido Brunetti, so she is the author behind the character.

clue.text: Crime writer put off by stabbing

indicators.note: a stabbing blade goes into its target, so one piece is driven inside the other

blocks.note: to deter someone is to put them off
by as in three by four, the multiplication sign

explanation.surface: A crime novelist is discouraged after witnessing a knife attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' looks like a link word; it is X, the sign read as 'by' in measurements like 2 by 4.
explanation.definitionFit: Colin Dexter wrote the Inspector Morse detective novels set in Oxford, so he is a well-known writer of crime fiction.

clue.text: 10, 4A wrote of one place to find it

blocks.note: first meaning: 4A, Penelope Fitzgerald, set a 1978 novel in a shop of this kind, and its title is this entry
second meaning: where you would go to buy her novel

explanation.surface: Fitzgerald wrote about a certain kind of shop, and that is where you can buy the book.
explanation.walkthrough: 4A is FITZGERALD; her 1978 novel The Bookshop concerns a woman opening one in a Suffolk town, and 'it' is that novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop selling books is both the setting of her novel and the obvious retail outlet for buying a copy.

clue.text: This US laureate is not minor or obscure

indicators.note: to obscure something is to muddy it, so the letters become jumbled

blocks.note: the twelve letters of these four words are the raw material

explanation.surface: A tribute insisting an American prize-winning writer is neither minor nor little known.
explanation.walkthrough: 'obscure' reads as an adjective paired with 'minor', but it is a verb telling us to scramble the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Toni Morrison, author of Beloved, received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993, making her an American Nobel laureate.

clue.text: A 4A piece in a paper backing socialist ends

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the abbreviation is written end to front

blocks.note: taken as written
the Financial Times, a British daily newspaper
red is a common label for a socialist
something that dies comes to an end

explanation.surface: A newspaper article by Fitzgerald supporting the aims of socialism.
explanation.walkthrough: 4A is FITZGERALD. 'backing' looks like support for the socialist, but it reverses the paper's initials; the FT is the Financial Times.
explanation.definitionFit: At Freddie's is Penelope Fitzgerald's 1982 novel about a London stage school for child actors, so it is one of her works.

clue.text: William of Baskerville visited these cooks to hold a bible class

indicators.note: holding something means keeping it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: to fry is to cook in fat
taken as written
RI is religious instruction, the old British school subject

explanation.surface: A sleuthing monk's tour of kitchens where the cooks run a scripture lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooks' reads as a noun, the kitchen staff; it is a verb, to fry. RI, religious instruction, was the British name for school religious education.
explanation.definitionFit: William of Baskerville is the Franciscan detective of Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose, and he travels between communities of brothers in monasteries.

clue.text: 14, 4A left this pub drunk once before church

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

blocks.note: an inn is a pub
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Fitzgerald walked out of the bar the worse for drink, just before a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' suggests walking out of the pub, but it means left behind as her legacy. CE is the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Innocence is Penelope Fitzgerald's 1986 novel set in Florence, one of the books the writer left behind her.

clue.text: Rudely, girls go topless around the French coves

indicators.note: to be topless is to lose your top, so the word's first letter is removed
being around something means encircling it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: bints is a vulgar British slang term for women, hence rudely
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Young women misbehaving by sunbathing topless in sheltered French bays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rudely' looks like an anagram signal, but it marks the slang word as a rude one: a dated, derogatory British term for women.
explanation.definitionFit: A cove and an inlet are both small sheltered bays where the sea runs into the coastline.

clue.text: Little people’s author brought back only Harry and Hermione

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: the trio is Harry, Ron and Hermione, so just the other two means leaving out Ron

explanation.surface: An author of a children's book about tiny people revives only two of the Hogwarts trio.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Potter's trio is Harry, Ron and Hermione; having only two of them is 'not Ron', reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Norton wrote The Borrowers, about a family of tiny people living under the floorboards, so she is their author.

clue.text: Bats star in the start of The Passage

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters go mad and rearrange
the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the six letters of these two words are the raw material
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Vampire-like bat creatures feature in the opening of Justin Cronin's horror novel The Passage.
explanation.walkthrough: The Passage looks like a book title, and Cronin's novel has bat-like monsters; but 'Passage' is the definition and 'Bats' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Transit means the act of passing across or through somewhere, which is a passage in the sense of a journey.

clue.text: Children‘s author, of Worzel, left hearts oddly lifted

indicators.note: lifting the odd-placed letters takes them away, so only the even ones remain

blocks.note: Barbara Euphan Todd wrote the Worzel Gummidge books about a walking scarecrow
L is the standard abbreviation for left
the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A children's writer, creator of the scarecrow Worzel Gummidge, leaves cheerfully uplifted spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly lifted' sounds like strangely raised spirits; it removes the odd letters of 'hearts'. Worzel Gummidge is a talking scarecrow from British children's books and television.
explanation.definitionFit: Toddlers are very young children just learning to walk, so the plural noun matches the plural definition.

clue.text: Two parts in Lear, but not the poor idiot

blocks.note: Edgar's disguise in Lear is the beggar Poor Tom; without the adjective only the name is left
the king's jester is the second of the two roles

explanation.surface: An actor may take two roles in King Lear, though not the role of the pitiful madman.
explanation.walkthrough: In King Lear, Edgar disguises himself as the beggar Poor Tom, and the king has a Fool. 'the poor' looks like Lear's wretched subjects, but it strips 'Poor' from Tom.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomfool is a foolish or stupid person, an old-fashioned word for a buffoon or simpleton.

clue.text: Sign a short bloke up for a part in Il Trovatore

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, the opposite way

blocks.note: Leo is a sign of the zodiac
taken as written
Ron is the short form of Ronald, a man's name

explanation.surface: An opera company signs up a short man to sing a role in Verdi's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign up' reads as recruiting; 'Sign' is the zodiac and 'up' reverses A plus RON.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonora is the soprano heroine of Verdi's opera Il Trovatore, loved by both Manrico and the Count di Luna.

clue.text: Switching mint candy for Christmas pudding was her idea

indicators.note: switching things around swaps their positions, so these letters change places

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, joined with the next word
this word also goes into the mix

explanation.surface: Someone thought of serving peppermint sweets instead of the traditional festive dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: Christmas Pudding is a 1932 comic novel by Nancy Mitford, eldest of the Mitford sisters; 'for' does double duty only in the surface, here it is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Her second novel was titled Christmas Pudding, so the book was her invention, making her the person whose idea it was.

clue.text: Rome’s split by this group bringing Caesar at last

indicators.note: at last points to the very end of a word, so its final letter is what counts

blocks.note: a tribe is a social group; its own R is taken out
the final letter of the emperor's name

explanation.surface: Ancient Rome is divided by a faction that brings Caesar to power at last.
explanation.walkthrough: TRIBE's R moves to the end, as if Caesar's last letter has been brought to the back of the group.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tiber is the river flowing through the middle of Rome, dividing the city into two banks.

clue.text: An Aussie writer’s detailed mind

indicators.note: de-tailed means having the tail cut off, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: Peter Carey, twice Booker winner, is an Australian novelist

explanation.surface: An Australian author has a meticulous, precise intellect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' reads as meticulous; it is de-tailed, losing the final letter. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To mind and to care are both verbs meaning to be concerned about or object to something, as in 'I don't mind'.

clue.text: Who chose the lead singing part and cropped bits?

indicators.note: cropping trims something short, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: the bass is the lowest voice part in a choir
taken as written, then trimmed
binary bits are ones and zeros, which look like these two letters

explanation.surface: A question about who picked the leading vocal role and the trimmed sections of a score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the lead' looks like a starring role; it is the metal. In The Merchant of Venice, Portia's suitors choose between gold, silver and lead caskets, and only he picks lead and wins her.
explanation.definitionFit: Bassanio is the suitor in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice who correctly chose the lead casket to win Portia's hand.

clue.text: Atkinson made this PI have too much cheese around

indicators.note: being around something means enclosing it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: Brie is a soft French cheese
OD is short for overdose

explanation.surface: A writer makes her private detective overindulge in cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: Atkinson may suggest Rowan Atkinson the comedian, but it is the novelist Kate Atkinson, whose detective series began with Case Histories.
explanation.definitionFit: Jackson Brodie is the private investigator hero of Kate Atkinson's crime novels, a former soldier and policeman.

clue.text: A writer could have one pint without lines by Tess getting muddled

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece sits round the other
muddled things are mixed up, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: a pint is a glass of beer in a British pub
L is an abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer might have a pint, going without any lines from Hardy's Tess while befuddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without lines' looks like 'lacking lines', but 'without' here has its old sense of outside, as in the hymn 'a green hill far away, without a city wall'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bestseller is a hugely popular book, the kind of hit that any writer could hope to produce.

clue.text: In times past, back end of chancel

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words, spanning the gap between them
going back means travelling the other way, so the letters read from right to left

blocks.note: these letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Historically, the rear part of a church's chancel served a particular role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In times past' reads as 'formerly'; it puts the answer inside 'times past', read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the semicircular vaulted recess at the eastern end of a church, usually beyond the chancel.
